pages.c01-p01: Describe the following programming paradigms: procedural programming; and object-oriented programming
pages.c01-p02: Describe the following programming paradigms: procedural programming; and object-oriented programming
pages.c01-p03: Explain the significance of the following aspects of software development environments: editing features; and high-level code translation and execution
pages.c01-p04: Explain the significance of the following aspects of software development environments: editing features; and high-level code translation and execution

q.q: What is a programming paradigm?
o: A set of grammar rules that a compiler checks the source code against before translation
A translator program that turns high-level source code into machine code for the CPU
A diagram that shows the order in which the procedures of a program are called
A style or approach to programming that decides how a problem is broken down and the code organised
q.why: A paradigm is a style or approach to programming. Grammar rules are syntax, and a translator is a compiler or interpreter.

q.q: Which two programming paradigms does the CCEA specification ask you to describe?
o: Procedural and object-oriented
Procedural and event-driven
Object-oriented and functional
Imperative and declarative
q.why: CCEA asks for procedural and object-oriented programming. Imperative is a feature of procedural code, not the second paradigm on the specification.

q.q: In procedural programming, what does it mean to say the code is imperative?
o: Every statement must be translated into machine code before the program runs
Every statement is grouped inside an object together with the data it uses
Every statement is a command telling the computer exactly what to do
Every statement is checked for errors by the IDE as soon as it is typed
q.why: Imperative means each statement is a command, such as input this, add that, output the result.

q.q: In a procedural program, what normally decides the flow of the program?
o: The order the statements are written in, changed only by selection and iteration
The order in which objects are created from their classes when the program starts
The order the compiler chooses after it has optimised the object code
The order in which the user clicks buttons and other controls on the form
q.why: Procedural code is sequential: the statements run in the order written, with selection and iteration altering that flow.

q.q: In procedural programming, how is the main task usually broken down?
o: Bottom-up, by first listing the objects in the problem and their properties
Top-down, into smaller sub-tasks that each become a procedure or function
Into classes that inherit methods from one another
Into tokens that are checked against the grammar of the language
q.why: Procedural design is top-down: the main task is split into sub-tasks, and each becomes a procedure or function.

q.q: A pupil writes: "Procedural programming means step-by-step instructions." According to examiners, why is this answer weak?
o: It is incorrect, because procedural programs are built from objects rather than step-by-step instructions
It is incorrect, because procedural programs do not run their statements in any particular order
It is only a Level 1 answer; it should also mention classes, encapsulation and inheritance
It is only a Level 1 answer; it should also mention imperative commands, procedures and functions, top-down design and data passed as parameters
q.why: Examiners said 'step-by-step instructions' alone is Level 1. Classes, encapsulation and inheritance describe OOP, not procedural programming.

q.q: How is data handled in a procedural program?
o: It is kept separate from the code in variables and passed into procedures and functions as parameters
It is kept inside each object and can only be changed through that object's own methods
It is stored in the executable file and read back each time a procedure is called
It is held in private fields and reached through public get and set properties
q.why: In procedural programming data is separate from the code and passed in as parameters. Private fields and properties belong to OOP.

q.q: What is the difference between a procedure and a function in the carpet calculator example?
o: A function returns a value, such as Area; a procedure carries out a task without returning a value, such as ShowBanner
A procedure returns a value, such as Area; a function carries out a task without returning a value, such as ShowBanner
A function can only be called once, but a procedure can be called as often as needed
A procedure is stored inside a class, but a function is stored in the main program
q.why: Area returns width * height, so it is a function; ShowBanner only outputs text, so it is a procedure.

o: A procedure, because it returns a value
A class, because it holds data
A function, because it returns a value
A property, because it has a get accessor
q.why: Area returns a double, so it is a function. A procedure does not return a value.

q.q: In the procedural carpet calculator, the main program stores the inputs in w and l and then calls Area(w, l). Why is this the clearest sign of the procedural style?
o: The data is hidden inside an object so that only its own methods can change it
The data lives in variables in the main program and is passed to the function, so data and code are kept separate
The function inherits the width and length from the main program automatically
The values are translated into machine code one line at a time as the program runs
q.why: Passing data held in variables into a function shows the separation of data and code that marks procedural programming.

q.q: Which type of task is procedural programming best suited to?
o: Smaller, linear tasks with a clear start and end, such as a calculation or a quiz
Large, complex systems with many interacting parts, such as games and GUIs
Programs where many programmers each build and test separate classes
Programs that must hide their data from every other part of the code
q.why: Procedural code suits smaller, linear tasks. Large systems, GUIs and games suit OOP.

q.q: Why can large procedural programs become harder to maintain?
o: Procedures cannot be called more than once, so code has to be copied many times
Procedural programs cannot use selection or iteration, so they grow very long
Many procedures may share and change the same data, so a change in one place can affect others
Procedural programs must be interpreted, so they run too slowly when they get large
q.why: The notes say that as programs grow, many procedures may share and change the same data, which makes them harder to maintain.

q.q: Which early high-level languages were designed around procedures?
o: C#, Java and Python
HTML, CSS and JavaScript
SQL, FORTRAN and HTML
FORTRAN, COBOL and C
q.why: FORTRAN (science), COBOL (business) and C were designed around procedures. C# supports both paradigms.

q.q: Which language was originally designed for business records and follows the procedural style?
o: FORTRAN
C
C#
COBOL
q.why: COBOL was designed for business records; FORTRAN was for science and engineering.

q.q: Which procedural language is still used to write operating systems and the software inside devices?
o: COBOL
FORTRAN
Python
C
q.why: The notes say C is still used for operating systems and the software inside devices.

q.q: A procedural program is described as "really a collection of procedures". What does the main program do?
o: It sets up the data and then calls the procedures in the right order
It creates objects from classes and lets them send messages to each other
It translates each procedure into machine code before the user runs it
It holds all of the code itself, so the procedures are never used
q.why: The main program sets up the data and calls the procedures in order.

q.q: Which feature of procedural programming lets the same block of code be used many times in a program?
o: Keeping data inside objects so it can only be changed through their methods
Grouping instructions into named procedures and functions that can be called from anywhere
Running every statement in the order it is written from top to bottom
Translating the whole program into an executable before it runs
q.why: Procedures and functions are named blocks that can be called as often as needed.

q.q: A programmer is writing a short program that asks for a test score and outputs a grade. Why might a procedural approach suit this task?
o: It is a small, linear task with a clear start and end, so procedural code is quick to write and easy to follow
It is a large system with many interacting objects, so procedural code protects the data best
Procedural code is the only style C# allows for programs that use selection
Procedural code produces an executable file, but object-oriented code cannot
q.why: Procedural code suits small, linear tasks. C# supports both styles, and both can be compiled.

q.q: Which C# keyword in a procedure header shows that it returns no value?
o: double
void
static
return
q.why: void means no value is returned, as in static void ShowBanner(). double is the return type of the Area function.

q.q: In procedural programming, what are values passed into a procedure or function called?
o: Properties
Fields
Tokens
Parameters
q.why: Data is passed into procedures and functions as parameters. Properties and fields belong to objects; tokens are made during lexical analysis.

q.q: Which list contains only features of procedural programming?
o: Imperative commands, classes, inheritance, top-down design
Objects, methods, encapsulation, data passed as parameters
Imperative commands, sequence, procedures and functions, top-down design
Sequence, encapsulation, procedures and functions, inheritance
q.why: The procedural key words are imperative, sequence, procedures and functions, top-down and data passed as parameters. Classes, encapsulation and inheritance are OOP.

q.q: Which statement about C# and programming paradigms is correct?
o: C# supports only object-oriented programming
C# supports both procedural and object-oriented programming
C# supports only procedural programming
C# supports neither paradigm, as it is a compiled language
q.why: The notes say C# supports both paradigms, so you write in both styles.

q.q: A program contains the line Console.WriteLine("Carpet needed: " + Area(w, l) + " m²"); What happens when this line runs?
o: The Area procedure is called, but nothing is output because procedures return no value
The Area function is called with w and l, and the value it returns is output as part of the message
The values of w and l are output, and Area is called afterwards
The Area method changes the private fields w and l inside an object
q.why: Area(w, l) is a function call; its returned value is joined into the message and output.

q.q: Which description of top-down design is correct?
o: Writing the program so that the first line typed is always the first to be translated
Starting the design by listing the objects in the problem and what they can do
Testing the program from the first line to the last line using a debugger
Breaking the main task into smaller sub-tasks, each of which becomes a procedure or function
q.why: Top-down design breaks the main task into sub-tasks that become procedures or functions.

q.q: In object-oriented programming, what question does the programmer ask first?
o: What steps are needed to solve this problem?
Which translator will be used to run this program?
Which procedures will share the same data?
What things (objects) are in this problem?
q.why: OOP design starts with the objects in the problem; procedural design starts with the steps.

q.q: What is a class?
o: One instance made from a blueprint, holding its own values for each property
A blueprint or template that defines what every object of that type will know and do
An action that an object can carry out, such as AddMerit()
A data item held inside an object, such as a pupil's form
q.why: A class is the blueprint. An object is an instance; a method is an action; a property is data.

q.q: What is an object?
o: A blueprint that defines the properties and methods of many classes
A named block of code that returns a value to the main program
One instance made from a class, with its own values
A template from which a class is created
q.why: An object is an instance of a class. 'An object is a template for a class' is the wrong way round.

q.q: Which statement about classes and objects is correct?
o: Many objects can be made from one class, each with its own values
Many classes can be made from one object, each with its own values
Only one object can ever be made from each class
A class and its objects must always hold exactly the same values
q.why: A class is a blueprint, and many objects with different values can be built from it.

q.q: In OOP, what are properties (attributes)?
o: The actions an object can carry out, such as Report()
The values passed into a procedure in the main program
The data an object holds, such as a pupil's name and form
The tokens produced when a class is compiled
q.why: Properties are data; methods are actions.

q.q: A Car class has Colour and Speed, and a routine called Brake(). What are Colour and Speed?
o: Methods
Objects
Parameters
Properties
q.why: Colour and Speed are data the car holds, so they are properties. Brake() is a method.

q.q: In OOP, how do objects work together?
o: By sharing global variables that every procedure can change
By copying each other's private fields directly
By calling each other's methods, sometimes called sending messages
By being translated one line at a time by an interpreter
q.why: Objects call each other's methods, described as sending messages.

o: One class (Pupil) and two objects (p1 and p2)
Two classes (p1 and p2) and one object (Pupil)
Two classes and two objects
One class and one object, as both lines create Pupil
q.why: Pupil is the single class; p1 and p2 are two separate objects (instances) made from it.

o: Aoife (11B) has 0 merits
Aoife (11B) has 2 merits
Aoife (11B) has 1 merits
Aoife has 2 merits
q.why: merits starts at 0 and AddMerit() is called twice, giving 2. Report includes the form in brackets.

o: Conor (11D) has 0 merits
Conor (11C) has 0 merits
Conor (11D) has 1 merits
Conor (11C) has 1 merits
q.why: The set accessor of Form changes the private field form to 11D. No merits were added, so merits is 0.

q.q: In the textbook's C# class layout, where is an object's data held?
o: In public fields that any code can change directly
In parameters passed in by the main program each time
In public methods that hold the values between calls
In private fields, reached through public properties
q.why: The data is held in private fields, and other code reaches it through public properties with get and set accessors.

q.q: In a C# property, what does the get accessor do?
o: It changes the private field to a new value
It creates a new object from the class
It hands the value of the private field out to other code
It deletes the value held in the field
q.why: get hands the value out; set lets it be changed.

q.q: In a C# set accessor such as set { form = value; }, what is value?
o: The keyword that holds the new value being assigned to the property
The name of the private field being changed
The value the property had before it was changed
A method that checks whether the new value is valid
q.why: In a set accessor the new value arrives in the keyword value.

q.q: The Pupil class has public string Name { get { return name; } } with no set accessor. What does this mean?
o: Other code can change a pupil's name, but cannot read it
Other code can both read and change a pupil's name at any time
Nothing outside the class can read or change a pupil's name
Other code can read a pupil's name, but cannot change it after the pupil is created
q.why: With only a get accessor, the property is read-only from outside the class.

q.q: In the Pupil constructor, the line this.name = name; appears. What does this.name refer to?
o: The parameter passed into the constructor
The field belonging to this object
A new object called name
The Name property's set accessor
q.why: this means this object, so this.name is the field and name on its own is the parameter.

q.q: What is encapsulation?
o: Keeping an object's data inside it so it can only be read or changed through the object's own properties and methods
Letting a new class take on all the properties and methods of an existing class and add its own
Breaking the main task into smaller sub-tasks, each becoming a procedure or function
Passing data held in variables into procedures and functions as parameters
q.why: Encapsulation (information hiding) protects an object's data. The second option describes inheritance.

q.q: In the Pupil class, merits is private and has no property; the only way to change it is AddMerit(). Which OOP feature does this show?
o: Inheritance
Iteration
Sequence
Encapsulation
q.why: Hiding merits so only AddMerit() can change it is encapsulation; no other code can set it to 500.

q.q: What is inheritance?
o: An object keeping its data private so that only its own methods can change it
A function receiving data from the main program as parameters
One class being used to create many objects with different values
A new class taking on all the properties and methods of an existing class and adding its own
q.why: Inheritance lets a class reuse and extend another class.

q.q: A Prefect class is created from the Pupil class and adds a Duty property, without rewriting any pupil code. Which OOP feature is this?
o: Inheritance
Encapsulation
Information hiding
Instantiation by constructor
q.why: Prefect inheriting all of Pupil and adding Duty is inheritance.

q.q: Which row correctly compares procedural and object-oriented programming?
o: Procedural combines data and code inside objects; OOP keeps them separate
Procedural design starts with the objects; OOP design starts with the steps
Procedural code is reused by inheritance; OOP code is reused only by calling functions
Procedural keeps data and code separate; OOP combines them inside each object
q.why: Procedural separates data and code; OOP combines them in objects. Design and reuse are the other way round in the wrong options.

q.q: A team is building a large game with players, enemies and levels, and several programmers will work on it at once. Which paradigm suits it best and why?
o: Object-oriented, because each class can be written and tested independently and reused
Procedural, because the steps of a game always run in a fixed order from start to finish
Procedural, because sharing the same data between many procedures reduces errors
Object-oriented, because object-oriented programs never need to be translated
q.why: OOP suits large, complex systems and games; classes can be developed independently by different programmers. All high-level programs must be translated.

q.q: Which of these is a benefit of OOP given in the notes?
o: Objects share all their data, so any part of the program can change any value quickly
A tested class can be reused in other programs, making large programs quicker to build and more reliable
Programs are always shorter, because classes cannot contain methods
Programs run line by line, so errors are easier to find
q.why: Reuse of self-contained, tested classes is a key OOP benefit; protected data, not shared data, reduces errors.

q.q: Why does encapsulation help to reduce errors in large programs?
o: Every object's data can be changed from anywhere, so mistakes are easy to correct
Other code cannot change an object's data directly, so values cannot be set wrongly from elsewhere
The compiler removes any object whose data has been changed by another class
Encapsulated code is translated one line at a time, so errors stop the program
q.why: Hidden internal details mean other code cannot change an object's data directly, which reduces errors.

q.q: When you drag a button onto a C# Windows Form, what have you created?
o: An object made from a class in the .NET library
A class that has no properties or methods
A procedure that runs whenever the program starts
A field inside the Program class
q.why: Every form, button and text box on a Windows Form is an object made from a .NET class.

q.q: Which statement would lose the mark in an exam answer about OOP?
o: A class is a blueprint for creating objects
An object is an instance of a class
Many objects can be made from one class
An object is a template for a class
q.why: The class is the blueprint and the object is built from it; 'an object is a template for a class' is the wrong way round.

q.q: What is an IDE?
o: An interpreter that translates and runs a program one line at a time
An editing feature that suggests keywords and method names as you type
An executable file produced by the compiler after translation
An integrated development environment: one application that holds every tool needed to develop a program
q.why: An IDE such as Visual Studio brings the editor, translator, debugger and other tools into one application.

q.q: Which IDE do you use to write C# on this course?
o: IntelliSense
.NET runtime
Visual Studio
Solution explorer
q.why: Visual Studio is the IDE. IntelliSense is one of its editing features and the solution explorer is one of its tools.

q.q: Which list contains only tools found in an IDE?
o: Code editor, CPU, debugger, main memory
Translator, operating system, keyboard, debugger
Code editor, translator, debugger, GUI designer
GUI designer, toolbox, CPU, compiler
q.why: An IDE includes the code editor, translator, debugger, GUI designer and toolbox, solution explorer and error list. The CPU and memory are hardware.

q.q: The specification asks you to explain the significance of IDE features. What does that mean?
o: Listing the features in the order they appear on the menu bar
Describing how each feature is translated into machine code
Saying how each feature helps the programmer, not just naming it
Naming as many features as possible in the time available
q.why: Significance means explaining how the feature helps, for example fewer errors or faster coding.

q.q: What does IntelliSense (auto-complete) do?
o: Suggests keywords, variable and method names as you type and shows the parameters a method needs
Shows keywords, strings, comments and numbers in different colours
Collapses and expands blocks such as methods, loops and IF statements
Draws a wavy red line under code that breaks the language rules
q.why: IntelliSense gives suggestions and parameter information as you type. The others are syntax highlighting, code outlining and error underlining.

q.q: Why is IntelliSense significant for a programmer?
o: Logic errors are found automatically before the program is compiled
Typing is faster and there are fewer spelling and syntax errors, as names do not have to be remembered
The program runs faster because the names are shorter in machine code
Long programs are easier to navigate because finished sections are hidden
q.why: IntelliSense gives faster typing and fewer spelling/syntax errors. It does not find logic errors.

q.q: A programmer types Console.Wr and a list appears offering WriteLine and Write. Which feature is this?
o: IntelliSense
Syntax highlighting
Code outlining
Clipboard ring
q.why: Suggesting names as you type is IntelliSense (auto-complete).

q.q: What does syntax highlighting do?
o: Shows keywords, strings, comments and numbers in different colours
Underlines code that breaks the language rules with a wavy red line
Highlights the partner of a bracket when the cursor is next to it
Highlights the line where a breakpoint has been set
q.why: Syntax highlighting colours different parts of the code.

q.q: A pupil forgets the closing quotation mark on a string, and the rest of the line stays the same colour as the string. Which feature has helped them spot the mistake?
o: Line numbering
Code outlining
Syntax highlighting
IntelliSense
q.why: With syntax highlighting, a missing quotation mark shows because the string colour runs on.

q.q: What does error underlining show, and when?
o: A wavy red line under code that breaks the language rules, as you type
A list of logic errors, after the program has finished running
A breakpoint marker where the program will pause during debugging
A line number beside every line, before the program is compiled
q.why: Error underlining shows syntax errors as you type, so they can be fixed before running.

q.q: Why is error underlining significant?
o: Logic errors are spotted and fixed before the program is tested
Syntax errors are spotted and fixed immediately, before you try to run the program
The program is translated faster because errors are removed automatically
Users of the finished program can see where errors happened
q.why: Error underlining catches syntax errors as you type. It cannot spot logic errors, which still follow the language rules.

q.q: An error message says there is a problem on line 47. Which editing feature helps the programmer find it quickly?
o: Code outlining
Syntax highlighting
Auto-indent
Line numbering
q.why: Line numbering lets you go straight to the line named in an error message.

q.q: Apart from finding errors, how else does line numbering help?
o: It lets the compiler translate lines in any order
It collapses lines into one so code is shorter
Programmers working in a team can refer to particular lines
It colours the lines so comments stand out
q.why: Line numbers let team members refer to lines when discussing code.

q.q: What does code outlining do?
o: Draws an outline around code that contains a syntax error
Indents blocks automatically and matches brackets
Collapses and expands blocks such as methods, loops and IF statements
Shows an outline of the parameters a method needs
q.why: Code outlining collapses and expands blocks so long programs are easier to navigate.

q.q: A program is 600 lines long, and the programmer wants to hide the methods that are already finished so she can concentrate on one part. Which feature should she use?
o: Clipboard ring
Line numbering
Error underlining
Code outlining
q.why: Code outlining lets you collapse finished sections.

q.q: A programmer has an extra closing brace } and cannot tell which block it belongs to. Which feature would make this easiest to see?
o: Syntax highlighting of keywords
The clipboard ring
IntelliSense parameter hints
Auto-indent and bracket matching
q.why: Bracket matching highlights the partner of a bracket and auto-indent shows structure, so mismatched { } are easy to see.

q.q: Which editing feature lets a programmer paste any one of the last few blocks of code they copied?
o: Code outlining
Clipboard ring
IntelliSense
Bracket matching
q.why: The clipboard ring remembers several recent copies.

q.q: What is the main use of the debugger?
o: Finding syntax errors as the code is typed by underlining them in red
Translating the whole program into an executable file
Suggesting method names and parameters while you type
Tracking down logic errors by setting breakpoints, stepping through code and watching variables
q.why: The debugger is the main tool for logic errors; error underlining handles syntax errors as you type.

q.q: What is a breakpoint?
o: A point set in the code where the program pauses so the programmer can inspect it
A point where the program crashes because of a run-time error
A line that the compiler skips during translation
A collapsed block of code hidden by code outlining
q.why: Breakpoints are set in the debugger to pause the program so you can step through and watch variables.

q.q: A program runs without crashing but gives the wrong total. Which IDE tool is the best choice for finding the cause?
o: Error underlining, which will show a red line under the wrong calculation
Syntax highlighting, which will colour the wrong calculation differently
The toolbox, which will replace the wrong calculation with a working one
The debugger, stepping through the code and watching the variables change
q.why: A wrong total is a logic error. Error underlining and highlighting only deal with breaking the language rules.

q.q: Which IDE tool lets you drag buttons, labels and text boxes onto a form?
o: GUI designer and toolbox
Solution explorer
Error list
Debugger
q.why: The GUI designer and toolbox let you drag controls onto a form.

q.q: What does the solution (project) explorer do in an IDE?
o: Lists the errors in a program with their line numbers
Organises all the files in a project
Suggests names and parameters as you type
Pauses the program at a chosen line
q.why: The solution explorer organises the project's files.

q.q: Which is the best exam answer to "Explain one benefit of syntax highlighting"?
o: Syntax highlighting is a feature of the IDE that colours the code
Syntax highlighting translates the code into machine code more quickly
Keywords, strings and comments appear in different colours, so code is easier to read and errors are easier to spot
Keywords appear in different colours, so the program will run faster
q.why: An 'explain' answer names what it does and adds the benefit: easier to read, easier to find errors.

q.q: Which pair correctly matches an IDE feature to its benefit?
o: Line numbering: syntax errors are fixed as you type
Code outlining: long programs are easier to navigate
Clipboard ring: keywords are shown in colour
IntelliSense: finished methods can be hidden
q.why: Code outlining makes long programs easier to navigate. The other benefits belong to error underlining, syntax highlighting and code outlining.

q.q: Where can you see a list of all the errors in a program with their line numbers?
o: The toolbox
The clipboard ring
The error list
The solution explorer
q.why: The error list shows errors with line numbers when the program is built and run inside the IDE.

q.q: Why do programmers usually write in a high-level language such as C#?
o: It uses English-like keywords, so it is easy to read, write and debug
The processor can execute it directly without translation
It is written in binary, so it runs faster than other languages
It is specific to one type of processor, so it is more efficient
q.why: High-level languages use English-like keywords. The CPU cannot run them directly, so they must be translated.

q.q: What is machine code?
o: English-like code written by a programmer in a language such as C#
Binary instructions specific to a type of processor, which the processor can execute
A list of tokens produced from source code during lexical analysis
An intermediate language that every type of processor can run
q.why: Machine code is binary instructions for a particular processor; it is the only code the CPU can execute.

q.q: Why must a C# program be translated before it can run?
o: The source code is too large to fit in main memory
The processor can only execute machine code
The translator removes any logic errors in the code
Translation adds the comments the user needs
q.why: The CPU only runs machine code, so high-level source code must be translated.

q.q: What is the general name for software that converts high-level source code into machine code?
o: A debugger
A translator
An editor
An executable
q.why: Compilers and interpreters are both translators.

q.q: What does a compiler do?
o: Translates and runs the program one line at a time
Runs the program and stops at the first error reached
Translates the whole program into machine code before it is run
Checks the program for logic errors while it runs
q.why: A compiler translates the whole program first; an interpreter works line by line.

q.q: What does an interpreter do?
o: Translates the whole program into an executable before running it
Links library code into an executable file
Translates and executes the program one line (statement) at a time
Produces object code that is kept separately from the source code
q.why: An interpreter translates and runs one line at a time and produces no executable.

q.q: Which translator produces a stand-alone executable file such as an .exe?
o: An interpreter
A debugger
A compiler
A lexical analyser
q.why: Only a compiler produces an executable file; a common error is to say an interpreter does.

q.q: Why does a compiled program run faster than an interpreted one?
o: The compiler removes all the loops from the program
No translation happens while it runs, because it was all translated beforehand
The compiled program is still in source code, so the CPU reads it directly
The compiler translates one line at a time as the program runs
q.why: Compiled code is already machine code, so no translation is needed at run time.

q.q: A games company wants to sell its program without letting customers see its source code. Which translator should it use and why?
o: An interpreter, because no executable file is produced that could be copied
A compiler, because users only need the executable file, not the source code
An interpreter, because it hides each line once it has been translated
A compiler, because it sends the source code to users in machine code and English
q.why: A compiled program can be given to users without the source code, which protects the programmer's work.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of a compiler?
o: The finished program runs slowly because it is translated every time
The user must have the translator installed to run the program
Compiling takes time and the program must be recompiled after every change
It produces no executable file, so the source code must be shared
q.why: Compiling takes time and must be repeated after changes. The other options describe interpreters.

q.q: How does a compiler report syntax errors?
o: One at a time, stopping at the first error and running the lines before it
As a list once it has finished, and the program will not compile until they are fixed
By underlining them as the programmer types each line
By pausing the running program at a breakpoint
q.why: A compiler lists all errors after compiling; an interpreter stops at the first error reached.

q.q: Why is an interpreter convenient while developing and testing a program?
o: It produces a fast executable that can be handed to users
It hides the source code from the user
It stops as soon as it meets an error and shows where it is
It finds all the errors and lists them at the end
q.why: Stopping at the line with the error makes errors easy to find during development.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of interpreted programs for the user?
o: They run more quickly, but the user must recompile them after every change
They run more slowly, and the user needs the interpreter installed and access to the source code
The user receives only an executable, so they cannot see how the program works
The user must translate the program into object code by hand
q.why: Interpreted programs are slower and need the interpreter plus the source code.

q.q: What is the difference between source code and object code?
o: Source code is the machine-code version; object code is the program the programmer types
Source code is the code inside objects; object code is the code inside procedures
Source code contains comments; object code is the same code with the comments still in it
Source code is the program the programmer types; object code is the machine-code version the compiler produces
q.why: Source code is typed by the programmer; the compiler produces object code (machine code).

q.q: What is the correct order of the compiler stages given in the notes?
o: Lexical analysis, include library code, semantic analysis, syntax analysis, code generation and optimisation
Include library code, syntax analysis, lexical analysis, code generation and optimisation, semantic analysis
Include library code, lexical analysis, syntax analysis, semantic analysis, code generation and optimisation
Syntax analysis, lexical analysis, semantic analysis, include library code, code generation and optimisation
q.why: The order is pre-processing (library code), lexical, syntax, semantic, then code generation and optimisation.

q.q: Which compiler stage splits the source code into tokens and throws away spaces and comments?
o: Syntax analysis
Semantic analysis
Code optimisation
Lexical analysis
q.why: Lexical analysis reads characters and makes tokens; syntax analysis then checks the tokens against the grammar.

q.q: At which compiler stage would a missing semicolon be found?
o: Lexical analysis
Syntax analysis
Semantic analysis
Code generation
q.why: Syntax analysis checks tokens against the grammar rules, so a missing ; or bracket is found there.

q.q: A program tries to store a string in an int variable. At which compiler stage is this detected?
o: Semantic analysis
Lexical analysis
Syntax analysis
Pre-processing
q.why: Semantic analysis checks that statements make sense, such as types matching and variables being declared.

q.q: A programmer uses a variable that has never been declared. Which compiler stage checks for this?
o: Syntax analysis
Semantic analysis
Lexical analysis
Code optimisation
q.why: Semantic analysis checks that every variable has been declared.

q.q: In C#, what does a line such as using System.IO; at the top of a file do?
o: Imports the source code of another program to be interpreted line by line
Tells the compiler to skip lexical analysis for that file
Declares a variable called System.IO for use in the program
Names a library of ready-made, already compiled code that the program needs
q.why: using directives name the libraries needed; the library code is included in the first compiler stage.

q.q: What happens during execution of a compiled program?
o: The source code is loaded into main memory and translated one line at a time by the processor
The compiler reads the source code and lists any syntax errors it finds
The machine-code instructions are loaded into main memory, where the processor fetches and carries them out one by one
The tokens are checked against the grammar rules of the language
q.why: Execution means loading the machine code into memory for the processor to fetch and execute.

q.q: For GCSE, how should C#, Python and JavaScript be classified?
o: C# as compiled; Python and JavaScript as interpreted
C# as interpreted; Python and JavaScript as compiled
All three as compiled languages
All three as interpreted languages
q.why: For GCSE treat C# as compiled and Python and JavaScript as interpreted.

q.q: Strictly, what does Visual Studio compile C# into?
o: An intermediate language, which the .NET runtime turns into machine code just before it runs
Machine code directly, which is stored in the source code file
Python, which is then interpreted line by line
Tokens, which are executed directly by the processor
q.why: C# compiles to an intermediate language; the .NET runtime converts that to machine code just before it runs.

q.q: Which row of the compiler/interpreter comparison is correct?
o: Output: compiler gives no file; interpreter gives an executable
Errors: compiler stops at the first error; interpreter lists all errors at the end
Speed: compiled programs are slower; interpreted programs are faster
Best for: compiler for distributing finished programs; interpreter for developing and testing
q.why: Compilers suit distributing finished programs and interpreters suit development. The other rows are reversed.

q.q: A pupil writes: "An interpreter creates an executable file that runs line by line." What is wrong with this answer?
o: An interpreter does create an executable, but it runs the whole program at once
Nothing is wrong; interpreters produce executables that are slower than compiled ones
Only a compiler produces an executable; an interpreter translates the source code every time it runs
Only a debugger produces an executable; an interpreter produces object code
q.why: An interpreter produces no executable file; only a compiler does.

q.q: How does having the translator built into an IDE help the developer?
o: The program no longer needs to be translated into machine code at all
Logic errors are corrected automatically during compilation
The program can be built and run with one click, with the error list and debugger available on the running program
The source code is hidden from the programmer once it has been compiled
q.why: The IDE lets you build and run with one click, see errors with line numbers and debug the running program.
